extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and informed readers interested in public opinion, political theory, journalism, and social psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, analysing, and responding to stereotypes and codified assumptions that shape public opinion and moral codes; explains how stereotypes simplify perception, how codes rest on assumed facts, and practical clues for detecting false absolutism in arguments and propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype as economizer and censor
rubrics_metrics.description: The stereotype economizes effort and focuses energy by providing simplified images of how things behave; but uncritically held, it censors out much that needs to be taken into account and may blind people when circumstances change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the American wartime stereotype which enabled rapid mobilisation (1917–18) but left no place for considering the fruits of victory; those who cried for a Carthaginian peace in 1919 or deplored Versailles in 1921. Note that the stereotype both accelerates action and omits questions about aims and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of divergence — when stereotype breaks down
rubrics_metrics.description: There is always a point where the stereotype and the facts part company; when blind spots move from the edge of vision to the center, the stereotype is shattered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When this happens effective response requires critics courageous enough to sound an alarm, leaders capable of understanding the change, and a people tolerant by habit; otherwise the stereotype will frustrate effort and waste energy (e.g., postwar anticlimax).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral damage when stereotypes collapse
rubrics_metrics.description: When a stereotype is shattered, the elements it had legitimately taken into account are often shipwrecked with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Bernard Shaw's critique of doctrines (Free Trade, Laissez-faire, Darwinism): once the stereotype turns into an excuse, its earlier useful insights may be destroyed along with it. Beware sweeping rejection that throws out useful parts with the false whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of expertness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness consists of multiplying the number of aspects one is prepared to discover and cultivating the habit of discounting one's expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts perceive many distinct aspects that a casual observer misses; but limited expertness can also exaggerate stereotyping by trying to force phenomena into familiar categories (e.g., cavalry experts failing at trench warfare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral codes rest on assumed pictures of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: At the core of every moral code is a picture of human nature, a map of the universe, and a version of history; the rules of the code apply insofar as those factual assumptions hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codes (personal, economic, legal, patriotic, international) implicitly assume psychology, sociology, and historical narratives. To evaluate a code, examine these background assumptions rather than only comparing ideals. Example: patriotic vs commercial codes assume different human motives during wartime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis versus myth in codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes influenced by science treat their conception of facts as hypotheses open to test; traditional or unexamined codes treat their conceptions as completed myths not demanding proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scientific-minded moralist is humble and seeks evidence; the mythic moralist is dogmatic and lacks criteria to separate truth from error. The distinguishing mark of a myth is equating fact and fable on the same plane of credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of applying general rules to particular cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Around every code there is a cloud of interpreters who deduce more specific cases — the difficulty is in deciding whether a present predicament is the one the lawgiver had in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: the commandment 'thou shalt not kill' requires interpreters to define self-defense; misapplication or misjudgment of facts (imagined attack, provocation) creates confusion. Evaluate whether the interpreters' definitions fit the concrete circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes load perception with sentiment and prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes are suffused with preference, affection, dislike, fears, lusts, and hope; they determine not only what we see but how we judge it emotionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we often 'see' a judgment before the evidence, prejudice shapes perception. The quality of thinking depends on whether prejudices evoke love of what is felt good or hatred of what is outside one's version of good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as moralized and codified facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A public opinion is primarily a moralized and codified version of the facts — the central pattern of stereotypes determines which group of facts we notice and how we interpret them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why news policy tends to support editorial policy and why partisans literally see different facts (e.g., capitalist vs socialist perceptions). To analyse public opinion, uncover the stereotype-pattern that filters and frames observed facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clue: internal contradiction reveals constructed stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid blanket use of different absolutist principles that contradict each other is a clue that an argument has been constructed to obliterate inconvenient facts rather than to seek truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ruritanian territorial claims invoking successive and conflicting principles (geography, historic right, reparation, cultural superiority, defense). Detecting a chain of contradictions shows the principle-based argument is masking factual issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clue: inability to take account of space (or practical constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to account for physical space, distance, or logistical constraints is a common sign that the stereotype is exerting precedence over facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: demands to 'reestablish an Eastern Front' by projecting the Japanese army from Vladivostok to Poland, ignoring 5,000 miles and broken transport — the stereotype of 'war on two fronts' overrode geographic reality. Test proposals against concrete spatial/logistical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection and over-reliance on vivid images
rubrics_metrics.description: We perceive the world as a combination of what is there and what we expect; vivid, familiar images can flood perception and cause misrecognition or hallucination-like errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everyday examples: mistaking a stranger for a friend by hat shape; in public affairs, historical models or standard visual images (e.g., 'war on two fronts') can make people mentally project inappropriate patterns onto current events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to vilify opposition and invent conspiracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Out of opposition people construct villains, conspiracies, and reductive explanations that fit their stereotype: profiteers, capitalist plots, foreign gold, spies, or agitators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanism censors alternate explanations and simplifies complex social phenomena into intentional plots; detection requires asking whether complex phenomena have been reduced to conspiratorial narratives that ignore structural or contextual facts.
